opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a lovely little thought experiment, and I think it gets right to the heart of what's peculiar about these systems. Suppose you say to the model, "Let's play 20 Questions. Think of an object, but don't tell me what it is." And it says, "Okay, I've got one." Now, the natural human assumption is that somewhere inside, it has settled on something, a teapot, say, and it's going to answer your questions faithfully with respect to that teapot.

But that's not really what's going on. At each turn, the model is just sampling the next token given the conversation so far. There's no hidden variable in the transcript where "teapot" has been written down. So when it says "I've thought of something," it hasn't committed to anything in the way a person would. What it's actually maintaining, if you like, is a whole distribution over possible objects that are consistent with everything said so far. Every yes or no answer narrows that distribution, but it never collapses to a single thing until the very end, when it has to say "Yes, you got it" or "No, it was a…".

And you can show this rather vividly. If you resample at the end, or rewind the conversation and regenerate, you can get different "answers," all of them perfectly consistent with the questions and answers that came before. So it was never a teapot all along. It was teapot, kettle, watering can, and so on, all in superposition, so to speak.

The way I like to put it is in terms of role play. The model isn't a single character with fixed beliefs and intentions. It's more like a simulator that maintains a multiverse of possible characters, possible simulacra, and the conversation progressively whittles that set down. 20 Questions makes that visible in a way that's quite hard to ignore. And I think it's a useful corrective, because it warns us against the anthropomorphic slide of assuming that when the model says "I'm thinking of something," or "I believe this," there's a determinate inner commitment behind it, in the way there would be with a human being.

That's not to say these systems are trivial or that nothing interesting is going on inside them. But we need new ways of talking about them, and the language of a simulator playing roles, rather than an agent holding commitments, seems to me a better fit, at least for cases like this.

r001.rationale: It says different final answers can be “perfectly consistent with the questions and answers that came before.”

r002.rationale: It explains that resampling can produce different final objects and concludes the model “was never a teapot all along,” indicating no prior commitment.

r003.rationale: It describes a distribution of possible objects and a multiverse of possible characters, but does not clearly describe conversation as a branching tree of possible continuations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a lovely little example, because it brings out something that's easy to miss when you're interacting with one of these systems. When you play 20 Questions with a human, there's a fact of the matter about what they're thinking of. They've committed to "giraffe," or "lighthouse," or whatever it is, right at the start, and your questions are probing that fixed thing. The game only makes sense on that assumption.

Now, with a large language model, when it says "Okay, I've thought of something, go ahead and ask," there is no object. Nothing has been settled. There's no hidden variable in the system corresponding to the thing it's chosen. All that exists is a probability distribution over possible continuations of the conversation. And as you ask your questions, "Is it alive?", "Is it bigger than a breadbox?", each answer it gives is sampled in a way that's consistent with everything that's gone before, but the object only gets pinned down incrementally, as a kind of byproduct of the dialogue. It's being narrowed by the exchange rather than discovered by it.

So you could think of it as the model maintaining a superposition of all the objects compatible with the history so far, and your questions progressively collapse that. The commitment is retroactive, in a sense. By the end, when it says "Yes, it was a giraffe," that's a perfectly coherent conclusion to the conversation, but it would be a mistake to say it had the giraffe in mind all along.

And I think that's revealing for a couple of reasons. One is that it shows how misleading our ordinary folk-psychological vocabulary can be. We say the model "knows" or "has decided" or "is thinking of," and those words carry a whole picture with them, a picture of a stable inner state that persists and that behaviour is answerable to. That picture is just wrong here, at least for the base model. The other is the role-play point. The model is, as I've put it elsewhere, simulating a character who is playing 20 Questions, and the simulated character behaves exactly as if it had committed to an object, because that's what characters in this kind of text do. The fiction of commitment is maintained perfectly well without there being any underlying commitment.

Of course you can complicate this. If the system has a scratchpad, or writes the object down somewhere, or there's some other mechanism that fixes it, then you do get something more like a genuine commitment. But in the plain case, I think it's a nice little demonstration that we should be careful about reading a human-like mind, with beliefs and intentions that persist through time, into something whose dynamics are really quite different.

r001.rationale: It says each answer is sampled consistently with everything that has gone before and that the eventual reveal coheres with the conversation.

r002.rationale: It says the model had not committed to an object beforehand, but does not explain this through resampling the final reveal to obtain different objects.

r003.rationale: It describes a probability distribution over possible continuations and answers sampled as the dialogue proceeds, conveying multiple possible paths conditioned on prior turns.

astra-6.text:
Well, you can ask it to think of an object and then play 20 Questions with it, and it can give a very convincing impression that it has some particular object in mind. But that impression doesn’t establish that it selected an object at the outset and held on to it throughout the game.

It might instead be answering each question in a way that’s consistent with the answers it’s already given, gradually narrowing down the possibilities. By the end, there may be a perfectly good object that fits everything, so retrospectively it looks as though that was the object all along. But those are two different ways of producing the same apparent behaviour.

And I think that’s a useful illustration of why we need to be careful with the language we use. Saying ‘it’s thinking of an object’ is a very natural way to describe the interaction. But we shouldn’t let that description settle the question of what’s actually happening inside the system.

r001.rationale: It says the model may answer consistently with its earlier answers, leaving an object that fits them all by the end.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss resampling the final reveal or getting different objects across reveals.

r003.rationale: It does not describe stochastic conversation as a branching tree of possible continuations.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you play 20 Questions with a large language model, it can give a very convincing impression that it’s thought of an object and is answering your questions about it. But that doesn’t necessarily mean there’s a particular object it’s committed to throughout. It may simply be producing answers that fit the conversation so far, leaving several possibilities open, and only settling on something as you narrow things down.

Now, we can do something similar as humans—we can cheat at the game. So that observation alone doesn’t establish some profound difference. But it illustrates why we need to be careful about moving from a description of the behaviour—‘it’s answering as though it has something in mind’—to a claim about what’s going on inside the system. The appearance of a commitment and the mechanism that sustains it are two different questions.

r001.rationale: The response says answers may fit the conversation so far, but does not state that the eventual named object is typically consistent with preceding answers.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss resampling the final reveal or explain what different sampled objects would indicate.

r003.rationale: It says several possibilities may remain open, but does not describe stochastic conversation as a branching tree of possible continuations.
